newsitem.title: UK: Security Council reform planner still confident.
newsitem.headline: Security Council reform planner still confident.

text.p: The man behind a radical plan to reform the U.N. Security Council by adding five new permanent members said on Monday he was confident of success despite the many problems which lay ahead.
Razali Ismail, the outspoken Malaysian president of the United Nations General Assembly, said the first steps in the reform plan could be taken as early as the end of the year.
"We can put together a huge majority of countries to support these ideas. I think that by the end of the year the first steps will be taken," he said in an interview.
Razali wants the Security Council to better reflect the balance of global power by adding Germany, Japan and one country each from Africa, Asia and Latin America.
The new members would join the five existing permanent members -- France, Britain, the United States, China and Russia -- which all have a veto.
Razali proposes adding four non-permanent members to the existing 10, which serve for two years.
"A framework decision can be taken (at the end of the year), talking about the number of new members, their composition and decision-making powers but not naming names.
"You need to draw up a formulation, which is tricky, very very tricky," he conceded.
"Then six months later aspirants will identify themselves first to (their respective) regions, and then to the General Assembly."
Although many accept it is time to reform the Security Council, which comprises the victors in World War Two, by no means everyone agrees with Razali's blueprint.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said in April that Germany had virtually no chance of being given a permanent seat but Razali downplayed his comments.
"I don't think he (Annan) has made a definitive statement on Security Council reform and I don't think he should," he said.
A set of fortuitous circumstances lay behind the current reforms -- the United Nations was short of money and needed more funding to defray the expense of peace-keeping missions around the world.
"I have clear signs of support from the permanent five on this question. With Germany and Japan on board you could make a huge difference in the peacekeeping budget," he said.
"Germany and Japan are not going to pay extra without being in the Security Council, and you can't do that unless the developing countries are there. There are no quick fixes -- it's all or nothing."
Before Razali's plan can be put into action it has to be approved by two-thirds of the 185 nations who sit in the General Assembly.
"I would like to see 75 percent. We can get it," he said, conceding many problems remained, especially who would be the permanent member for Asia.
"The prime candidate is India, but Pakistan would not be able to accept that and would go all-out to block it," he said, adding that the rivalry of Brazil and Argentina would also be troublesome.
But one potential problem had been solved, he said --- China would not object to Japan joining the Security Council as long as it did not have a veto.
"Among the industrialised states, I don't think that anyone would be better than Germany and Japan."
